claim: Hierarchical temporal dynamics are a fundamental computational property of the brain.
source: Hierarchical temporal dynamics are a fundamental computational property of the brain; however, there are no whole brain, noninvasive investigations into timescales of neural processing in animal models.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract and introduction, drawing from established scientific consensus.

claim: There are no whole brain, noninvasive investigations into timescales of neural processing in animal models prior to this study.
source: Hierarchical temporal dynamics are a fundamental computational property of the brain; however, there are no whole brain, noninvasive investigations into timescales of neural processing in animal models.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Ultrahigh field functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) performed at 10.5 T was used to probe timescales across the whole macaque brain.
source: To that end, we used the spatial resolution and sensitivity of ultrahigh field functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) performed at 10.5 T to probe timescales across the whole macaque brain.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: There is within-species consistency between timescales estimated from fMRI and electrophysiology.
source: We uncovered within-species consistency between timescales estimated from fMRI and electrophysiology.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the comparison data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Existing electrophysiological hierarchies were extended to whole-brain topographies.
source: Crucially, we extended existing electrophysiological hierarchies to whole-brain topographies.
evidence: This is stated as a key contribution of the study.

claim: One facet of the high-dimensional functional connectivity (FC) topography of any region in the brain is closely related to hierarchical temporal dynamics.
source: Further, with these results in hand, we were able to show that one facet of the high-dimensional functional connectivity (FC) topography of any region in the brain is closely related to hierarchical temporal dynamics.
evidence: This is a major finding of the study, supported by the gradient analysis presented in Figures 3-5.

claim: Intrinsic timescales are organized along spatial gradients that closely match FC gradient topographies across the whole brain.
source: We demonstrated that intrinsic timescales are organized along spatial gradients that closely match FC gradient topographies across the whole brain.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the gradient analyses shown in Figures 3-5.

claim: Intrinsic timescales are a unifying organizational principle of neural processing across the whole brain.
source: We conclude that intrinsic timescales are a unifying organizational principle of neural processing across the whole brain.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on the integration of all findings.

claim: Fast-changing sensory input is encoded by the fast dynamics of sensory areas.
source: Hierarchical temporal dynamics are a fundamental computational property of the brain—fast-changing sensory input is encoded by the fast dynamics of sensory areas, which is in turn integrated into temporally extended representations encoded by the slower dynamics of higher-order areas (Cavanagh et al., 2020; Raut et al., 2020; Soltani et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Sensory information is integrated into temporally extended representations encoded by the slower dynamics of higher-order areas.
source: Hierarchical temporal dynamics are a fundamental computational property of the brain—fast-changing sensory input is encoded by the fast dynamics of sensory areas, which is in turn integrated into temporally extended representations encoded by the slower dynamics of higher-order areas (Cavanagh et al., 2020; Raut et al., 2020; Soltani et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Temporal integration and information processing over multiple timescales are crucial for understanding how the brain deals with the complexity of the real world.
source: Temporal integration and information processing over multiple timescales are crucial for understanding how the brain deals with the complexity of the real world (Zimmermann et al., 2018); hence, understanding whole-brain temporal dynamics is highly important.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Neural processing reflects a hierarchy of progressively longer 'temporal receptive windows' (TRWs) as one moves from sensory to associative areas.
source: As one moves from sensory to associative areas, neural processing reflects a hierarchy of progressively longer 'temporal receptive windows' (TRWs)—defined as the length of time during which an area accumulates information during task performance (Hasson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Temporal receptive windows (TRWs) are defined as the length of time during which an area accumulates information during task performance.
source: As one moves from sensory to associative areas, neural processing reflects a hierarchy of progressively longer 'temporal receptive windows' (TRWs)—defined as the length of time during which an area accumulates information during task performance (Hasson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a definition provided with citation support.

claim: Sensory areas have short TRWs to enable fast sensory processing.
source: In other words, the range of the TRW of each area reflects its functional role, with sensory areas having short TRWs, to enable fast sensory processing, and associative areas having longer TRWs, allowing them to process information unfolding over longer periods of time.
evidence: This is stated as an established principle in the field.

claim: Associative areas have longer TRWs, allowing them to process information unfolding over longer periods of time.
source: In other words, the range of the TRW of each area reflects its functional role, with sensory areas having short TRWs, to enable fast sensory processing, and associative areas having longer TRWs, allowing them to process information unfolding over longer periods of time.
evidence: This is stated as an established principle in the field.

claim: Temporal specialization arises from a region's intrinsic dynamics, present even in the absence of direct sensory stimulation.
source: Not only does neural processing display these timescales during task performance, but we now know that temporal specialization arises from a region's intrinsic dynamics, that is, temporal dynamics that are present even in the absence of direct sensory stimulation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Murray et al., 2014 first described intrinsic timescales by analyzing action potentials of single neurons in the macaque.
source: This was first described by Murray et al., 2014 analyzing action potentials of single neurons in the macaque.
evidence: This is a citation to the original work that described intrinsic timescales.

claim: Timescales of baseline neuronal activity vary across cortical areas, revealing a hierarchical progression from fast timescales in sensory areas to slower timescales in association areas.
source: They showed that timescales of baseline neuronal activity vary across cortical areas, revealing a hierarchical progression from fast timescales in sensory areas, to slower timescales in association areas.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Murray et al., 2014.

claim: Intrinsic fluctuations in the neural signal (intrinsic neural timescales, INTs) are thought to set the duration over which brain regions integrate inputs.
source: These intrinsic fluctuations in the neural signal, also described as intrinsic neural timescales (INTs), are thought to set the duration over which brain regions integrate inputs (Murray et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Murray et al., 2014.

claim: INTs are hypothesized to be the result of multiple neuronal mechanisms, including local dynamics and recurrent connectivity.
source: They are hypothesized to be the result of multiple neuronal mechanisms, including local dynamics and recurrent connectivity (Murray et al., 2014; Soltani et al., 2021; Watanabe et al., 2019; Demirtaş et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Additional studies have replicated and extended the INT hierarchy.
source: Additional studies have replicated and extended the INT hierarchy, reinforcing the idea that brain regions exhibit unique timescales in their intrinsic activity, which reflect functional specialization in terms of temporal integration (Cavanagh et al., 2016; Cirillo et al., 2018; Fascianelli et al., 2019; Murray et al., 2014; Ogawa and Komatsu, 2010; Rossi-Pool et al., 2021; Maisson et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The concept of INT hierarchy has been extended to subcortical regions, specifically the basal ganglia.
source: The concept of INT hierarchy has even been extended to subcortical regions—specifically the basal ganglia (Nougaret et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nougaret et al., 2021.

claim: A large-scale network model based on anatomical connectivity (AC) and the strength of local recurrent connectivity has been used to successfully reproduce the temporal hierarchy.
source: Moreover, a large-scale network model, based on anatomical connectivity (AC) and the strength of local recurrent connectivity, has been used to successfully reproduce the temporal hierarchy (Chaudhuri et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chaudhuri et al., 2015.

claim: Anatomical connectivity (AC) is closely related to INTs.
source: This suggests that AC is closely related to INTs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling work cited.

claim: Alterations in hierarchical INT patterns can result in cognitive and behavioral abnormalities.
source: Alterations in hierarchical INT patterns can result in cognitive and behavioral abnormalities (Watanabe et al., 2019; Wengler et al., 2020; Zilio et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Abnormal INT patterns have been associated with core symptoms of high-functioning individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder.
source: For example, abnormal INT patterns have been associated with core symptoms of high-functioning individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (Watanabe et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Watanabe et al., 2019.

claim: Delusions and hallucinations are associated with INT alterations at different hierarchical levels, leading to symptom-specific changes in hierarchical INT gradients.
source: Likewise, delusions and hallucinations are associated with INT alterations at different hierarchical levels, leading to symptom-specific changes in hierarchical INT gradients (Wengler et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wengler et al., 2020.

claim: Investigations into INTs have the potential to clarify hierarchical dysfunction in whole-brain dynamics in neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: Hence, investigations into INTs have the potential to clarify hierarchical dysfunction in whole-brain dynamics in neuropsychiatric disorders.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies showing INT alterations in disorders.

claim: INTs have traditionally been investigated using invasive electrophysiology.
source: Traditionally, INTs have been investigated using invasive electrophysiology, which is not suited to uncover whole-brain dynamics.
evidence: This is stated as established practice in the field.

claim: Invasive electrophysiology is not suited to uncover whole-brain dynamics.
source: Traditionally, INTs have been investigated using invasive electrophysiology, which is not suited to uncover whole-brain dynamics.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the traditional approach.

claim: Electrophysiology is challenging to collect in humans, particularly for large data sets.
source: It is also challenging to collect in humans, particularly for large data sets (as would be needed to assess differences across populations).
evidence: This is stated as a practical limitation of electrophysiology in humans.

claim: fMRI offers whole-brain coverage and can be performed across species and in larger sample sizes.
source: One way to overcome this problem is using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which offers whole-brain coverage and can be performed across species and in larger sample sizes.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of fMRI over electrophysiology.

claim: It is not yet clear whether hemodynamic INTs derived from fMRI reflect similar neural phenomena as those derived from electrophysiology.
source: However, it is not yet clear whether hemodynamic INTs derived from fMRI reflect similar neural phenomena as those derived from electrophysiology.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Electrophysiological and hemodynamic INTs must be compared directly within the same species to clarify whether hemodynamic INTs reflect similar neural phenomena.
source: To clarify this issue, electrophysiological and hemodynamic INTs must be compared directly within the same species.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological requirement for validation.

claim: Recent advancements in nonhuman primate (NHP) neuroimaging based on the use of very high magnetic fields (10.5 T) significantly boost signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs).
source: To that end, recent advancements in nonhuman primate (NHP) neuroimaging, based on the use of very high magnetic fields (10.5 T) for significantly boosting signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) (Lagore et al., 2021; Yacoub et al., 2020), make it possible to study hemodynamic INTs in the macaque brain.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent technical developments.

claim: Very high magnetic fields (10.5 T) make it possible to study hemodynamic INTs in the macaque brain.
source: To that end, recent advancements in nonhuman primate (NHP) neuroimaging, based on the use of very high magnetic fields (10.5 T) for significantly boosting signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) (Lagore et al., 2021; Yacoub et al., 2020), make it possible to study hemodynamic INTs in the macaque brain.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent technical developments.

claim: There is significant heterogeneity within regions in terms of INTs.
source: This is important since more recent work has shown that there is significant heterogeneity within regions (Cavanagh et al., 2020; Cirillo et al., 2018; Nougaret et al., 2021), even though initially INTs were assigned to cortical regions as a whole.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Gradients of functional connectivity (FC) can describe the functional architecture of neural processing.
source: In addition to INTs, gradients of functional connectivity (FC) can also describe the functional architecture of neural processing (Haak et al., 2018; Vos de Wael et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Gradient approaches map macroscale brain features to low-dimensional manifold representations.
source: Gradient approaches map macroscale brain features to low-dimensional manifold representations (Vos de Wael et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vos de Wael et al., 2020.

claim: Gradient mapping has the potential to uncover overlapping functional topographies by treating the high-dimensional connectivity structure as a spatial variance decomposition problem.
source: Gradient mapping has the potential to uncover overlapping functional topographies by treating the high-dimensional connectivity structure as a spatial variance decomposition problem.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the gradient mapping approach.

claim: Areas in the early visual cortex exhibit at least two gradual modes of functional change (eccentricity and polar angle maps).
source: For example, areas in the early visual cortex are known to exhibit at least two gradual modes of functional change (i.e., eccentricity and polar angle maps), which can be successfully retrieved from resting-state FC via gradient mapping (Haak et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Haak et al., 2018.

claim: The existence of multiple overlapping principles of topographic organization is likely a general property of the whole brain.
source: The existence of multiple overlapping principles of topographic organization is likely a general property of the whole brain (Haak et al., 2018; Harvey et al., 2020; Jbabdi et al., 2013; Marquand et al., 2017; Przezdzik et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Murray et al., 2014 initially described a visual cortical hierarchy of seven cortical areas in macaques.
source: Murray et al., 2014 initially described (in macaques) a visual cortical hierarchy of seven cortical areas: middle temporal (MT) area, lateral intraparietal (LIP) area, orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), lateral PFC (LPFC), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC); and a somatosensory hierarchy including primary somatosensory (S1) and secondary somatosensory (S2) cortex (Figure 1A–B, left).
evidence: This is a citation to the original work describing these hierarchies.

claim: The cortical hierarchy has been replicated and further extended by assigning INTs to the dorsal premotor (PMd) cortex, frontopolar cortex (PFp), ventral and dorsal LPFC (VLPFC and DLPFC).
source: This cortical hierarchy has been replicated and further extended by assigning INTs to the dorsal premotor (PMd) cortex, frontopolar cortex (PFp), ventral and dorsal LPFC (VLPFC and DLPFC) (Cavanagh et al., 2016; Cirillo et al., 2018; Fascianelli et al., 2019; Figure 1C–D, left).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: INTs have been estimated in the medial wall of the PFC, including the ventromedial PFC (vmPFC), subgenual ACC (sgACC), pregenual ACC (pgACC), and dorsal ACC (dACC).
source: Recently, INTs have been estimated in the medial wall of the PFC, including the ventromedial PFC (vmPFC), subgenual ACC (sgACC), pregenual ACC (pgACC), and dorsal ACC (dACC) (Maisson et al., 2021; Figure 1E, left).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Maisson et al., 2021.

claim: A subcortical INT hierarchy has been described for regions of the basal ganglia: external segment of the globus pallidus (GPe), subthalamic nucleus (STN), and the striatum.
source: Finally, a subcortical INT hierarchy has been described for regions of the basal ganglia: external segment of the globus pallidus (GPe), subthalamic nucleus (STN), and the striatum (Nougaret et al., 2021; Figure 1F, left).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nougaret et al., 2021.

claim: The electrophysiology-based and fMRI-based INTs reveal similar hierarchies across the brain.
source: The electrophysiology-based (Figure 1, left) and fMRI-based (Figure 1, right) INTs reveal similar hierarchies across the brain.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the comparison shown in Figure 1.

claim: fMRI is well-suited to investigate aspects of whole-brain temporal dynamics.
source: By replicating these physiological hierarchies, we demonstrate that fMRI is well-suited to investigate aspects of whole-brain temporal dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the replication of electrophysiological hierarchies with fMRI.

claim: Minor deviations from hierarchies estimated from single-unit recordings can be attributed to several factors such as a high degree of INT heterogeneity within these regions, and differences between studies in the atlases used and size of the areas under investigation.
source: Minor deviations from hierarchies estimated from single-unit recordings (e.g., in STN, sgACC, and pgACC) can be attributed to several factors such as a high degree of INT heterogeneity within these regions, and differences between studies in the atlases used and size of the areas under investigation (see Figure 1—figure supplement 3 for the INT stability analysis).
evidence: This is an interpretation of observed deviations, supported by reference to supplementary analysis.

claim: The lag-1 ACF values systematically varied across the brain.
source: In line with previous results, the lag-1 ACF values systematically varied across the brain (Shinn et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shinn et al., 2021.

claim: The lag-1 ACF values and the 0-crossing lag were linearly related to INTs as operationalized in this study.
source: Moreover, the lag-1 ACF values and the 0-crossing lag were linearly related to INTs as operationalized in this study (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for voxel-wise whole-brain maps of the lag-1, 0-crossing lag, and INTs).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Magnitude and timescale are closely related.
source: The maps suggest that magnitude and timescale are closely related.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis of lag-1 ACF values and 0-crossing lag.

claim: The hierarchical ordering of both cortical and subcortical areas based on 0-crossing lag is consistent with that based on the INT measure.
source: The hierarchical ordering of both cortical and subcortical areas is consistent (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2) with that based on our INT measure (see Figure 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Temporal hierarchies are not driven by heterogeneity in the ACF magnitude.
source: Hence, while the ACF magnitude is closely related to our INT index and the 0-crossing lag, temporal hierarchies are not driven by heterogeneity in the ACF magnitude.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of ACF magnitude and timescale components.

claim: A hierarchy of INTs exists in the dorsal visual pathway.
source: Specifically, we reveal a hierarchy of INTs in the dorsal visual pathway (Goodale et al., 1994; Goodale and Milner, 1992; Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: INTs gradually increase from the entry point of visual information to higher-order areas involved in visuo-motor integration in the dorsal visual pathway.
source: INTs gradually increase from the entry point of visual information to higher-order areas involved in visuo-motor integration (Figure 2, inset).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2.

claim: INTs are hierarchically organized within the occipito-parietal, parieto-premotor, and parieto-prefrontal components of the dorsal pathway.
source: INTs are hierarchically organized within the occipito-parietal, parieto-premotor, and parieto-prefrontal components of the dorsal pathway (Kravitz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis, with citation to the anatomical framework.

claim: The occipito-parietal pathway is the source of the other two pathways and is lower in the hierarchy.
source: Also, in line with the occipito-parietal pathway being the source of the other two pathways, it is lower in the hierarchy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the hierarchical organization observed.

claim: In the frontal lobe, the first component (G1) shows an overall anterior-posterior organization spanning from sensory to motor areas.
source: In the frontal lobe, the first component (i.e., G1) shows an overall anterior-posterior organization spanning from sensory to motor areas.
evidence: This is a finding from the gradient analysis of the frontal lobe.

claim: The anterior-posterior functional gradient in the frontal lobe aligns with previous studies.
source: This aligns with previous studies showing a global anterior-posterior functional gradient in the frontal lobe (Badre, 2008; Riley et al., 2018; Tan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the frontal lobe, the second component (G2) shows an overall lateral-medial organization, extending from the PMv to the medial wall.
source: The second component (i.e., G2) shows an overall lateral-medial organization, extending from the PMv to the medial wall.
evidence: This is a finding from the gradient analysis of the frontal lobe.

claim: The frontal INT map was correlated with G2 for both within-area (r=0.47) and fronto-parietal (r=–0.26) connectivity.
source: The INT map was correlated with G2 for both within-area (r=0.47) and fronto-parietal (r=–0.26) connectivity.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: In the parietal lobe, G1 showed a medial-lateral and G2 a ventro-dorsal overall organization.
source: In the parietal lobe, G1 showed a medial-lateral and G2 a ventro-dorsal overall organization.
evidence: This is a finding from the gradient analysis of the parietal lobe.

claim: The parietal INT map was correlated with G1 for both within-area (r=0.56) and fronto-parietal (r=0.47) connectivity.
source: The INT map was correlated with G1 for both within-area (r=0.56) and fronto-parietal (r=0.47) connectivity.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: The sign of the gradients is arbitrary as a byproduct of the decomposition method.
source: (Note that the sign of the gradients is arbitrary as a byproduct of the decomposition method [Haak and Beckmann, 2020]; hence, only the magnitude but not the direction of the INT-FC gradient correlation is relevant.)
evidence: This is a methodological note supported by a citation.

claim: In all functionally meaningful subdivisions of the frontal lobe examined, the INT maps were highly correlated with one of the principal components estimated from within-area connectivity.
source: In all cases, the INT maps were highly correlated with one of the principal components estimated from within-area connectivity (i.e., LPFC G1: r=0.35; Motor G1: r=0.68; OFC G2: r=0.45; MPFC G1: r=0.49).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: The motor cortex has a well-established hierarchy, with premotor regions at the top and M1 at the bottom.
source: For example, the motor cortex has a well-established hierarchy, with premotor regions at the top and M1 at the bottom (Binkofski and Buxbaum, 2013; Wong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The motor cortex INT and FC gradient maps reflected the functional hierarchy, with M1 being at one end and the PMv at the other.
source: Accordingly, the maps reflected this functional hierarchy, with M1 being at one end and the PMv at the other.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of motor cortex.

claim: The OFC shows a predominantly anterior-posterior axis of change.
source: The OFC shows a predominantly anterior-posterior axis of change, which agrees with anatomical findings—the caudal and lateral regions are more input-like unimodal regions while more anterior areas integrate these multimodal signals (Carmichael and Price, 1994; Carmichael and Price, 1996; Ongür and Price, 2000; Price, 1999).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis, supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The lateral and medial subdivisions of the PFC revealed a predominately anterior-posterior organization.
source: The lateral and medial subdivisions of the PFC revealed a predominately anterior-posterior organization.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of PFC subdivisions.

claim: The whole-cortex INT map was highly correlated with the second gradient estimated from the cortical FC matrix (r=0.70).
source: The whole-cortex INT map was highly correlated with the second gradient estimated from the cortical FC matrix (r=0.70).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the whole-cortex analysis.

claim: INTs and FC gradients are closely related and represent a functional principle of organization across the whole brain.
source: With these results in hand, we conclude that INTs and FC gradients are closely related and represent a functional principle of organization across the whole brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the multiple analyses showing INT-FC gradient correlations.

claim: The striatal INT map was correlated with the FC gradient estimated from cortico-striatal (r=0.38) connectivity.
source: The striatal INT map was correlated with the FC gradient estimated from cortico-striatal (r=0.38) connectivity (see Figure 5).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the cortico-striatal analysis.

claim: The cortico-striatal FC topography exhibited a gradual pattern of connectivity change corresponding to the anterior-posterior, dorsal-ventral, and medial-lateral anatomical gradient of connectivity derived from tract-tracing studies in NHPs.
source: The cortico-striatal FC topography exhibited a gradual pattern of connectivity change corresponding to the anterior-posterior, dorsal-ventral, and medial-lateral anatomical gradient of connectivity derived from tract-tracing studies in NHPs (Haber, 2016; Haber and Knutson, 2010; Friedman et al., 2002; Alexander et al., 1986).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis, supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Striatal INTs followed a similar pattern to the cortico-striatal FC gradient.
source: INTs followed a similar pattern.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the striatal analysis.

claim: The FC gradients were similar to those estimated from human neuroimaging data.
source: Moreover, the FC gradients were similar to those estimated from human neuroimaging data (Marquand et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Marquand et al., 2017.

claim: The cortico-striatal FC closely matched AC.
source: This analysis not only validated the meaning of the gradients, but also revealed that the cortico-striatal FC closely matched AC.
evidence: This is a finding from the cortical projection analysis.

claim: The striatal INTs and reconstructed cortico-striatal INT maps were correlated (r=0.45).
source: In accordance with the above-mentioned results, the striatal INTs and reconstructed cortico-striatal INT maps were correlated (r=0.45).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the INT reconstruction analysis.

claim: At the voxel level, the INT values closely matched the average INTs of their top 10 strongest cortical connections.
source: At the voxel level, the INT values closely matched the average INTs of their top 10 strongest cortical connections.
evidence: This is a finding from the voxel-level analysis.

claim: INTs are topographically organized along FC gradients throughout the NHP brain.
source: We show that INTs are topographically organized along FC gradients throughout the NHP brain.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the multiple analyses presented.

claim: Resting-state temporal and spatial dynamics are closely related.
source: Although we focused our analysis on the frontal and parietal lobes, and the striatum, we also showed that a whole-brain analysis recapitulates the same conclusion: resting-state temporal and spatial dynamics are closely related.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the whole-brain analysis.

claim: Hemodynamic INTs derived from fMRI in human subjects were validated with EEG in a previous paper.
source: Furthermore, in a previous paper, INTs derived from fMRI data in human subjects were elegantly validated with EEG (Watanabe et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a citation to previous validation work.

claim: The present findings find slower and faster INTs in frontoparietal areas and sensory-related areas, respectively, in agreement with human results.
source: The present findings are in agreement with these results, finding slower and faster INTs in frontoparietal areas and sensory-related areas, respectively.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings with previous human results.

claim: The present findings point toward cross-species homologies in cortical INTs.
source: This points toward cross-species homologies in cortical INTs, hence, laying the groundwork for future translational work.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of findings across species.

claim: The equivalence of fMRI estimates of INT hierarchies with single-neuron spiking results within the same species provides validation for the complementary use of hemodynamic and electrophysiological INTs.
source: Nevertheless, the step presented here is essential, because we were able to demonstrate the equivalence of the fMRI estimates of INT hierarchies with single-neuron spiking results within the same species. This finding provides validation for the complementary use of hemodynamic and electrophysiological INTs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the within-species validation.

claim: Minor deviations from electrophysiological INTs may be in large part attributable to a high degree of INT heterogeneity within individual anatomical regions.
source: We did observe minor deviations from electrophysiological INTs in our data. These may be in large part attributable to a high degree of INT heterogeneity within individual anatomical regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of observed deviations.

claim: The observation of INT heterogeneity within regions is in line with previous reports of heterogeneity within neural populations in single-unit recordings.
source: This observation is in line with previous reports of heterogeneity within neural populations in single-unit recordings (Cirillo et al., 2018; Nougaret et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Averaging INTs within anatomical regions might not provide a full description of macroscale organization.
source: This suggests that averaging INTs within anatomical regions might not provide a full description of macroscale organization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed heterogeneity.

claim: The current study could not resolve the exact correspondence between the time constants estimated from spiking activity and BOLD.
source: It is worth noting that the current study could not resolve the exact correspondence between the time constants estimated from spiking activity and BOLD.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: A spatially localized increase in the fMRI signal directly and monotonically reflects an increase in neural activity, with the mean onset time of the BOLD signal relative to the neural activation being 2 s.
source: The relationship between neural activity and the BOLD signal has been revealed via simultaneous electrophysiological-fMRI recording—that is, a spatially localized increase in the fMRI signal directly and monotonically reflects an increase in neural activity, with the mean onset time of the BOLD signal relative to the neural activation being 2 s (Logothetis et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Logothetis et al., 2001.

claim: Local field potentials (LFPs), and to a lesser extent multiunit activity, can predict the BOLD signal when convolved with the neuro-vascular impulse response function.
source: Local field potentials (LFPs), and to a lesser extent multiunit activity, can predict the BOLD signal when convolved with the neuro-vascular impulse response function.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the BOLD signal.

claim: The hemodynamic response is roughly a low-pass-filtered expression of the total neural activity, with LFPs having a greater contribution to the signal.
source: In sum, the hemodynamic response is roughly a low-pass-filtered expression of the total neural activity; with LFPs, however, having a greater contribution to the signal.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the hemodynamic response.

claim: Hemodynamic timescales are more likely to reflect timescales related to LFPs rather than spiking activity.
source: This has several implications for the interpretation of hemodynamic timescales: (1) they are more likely to reflect timescales related to LFPs rather than spiking activity
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between BOLD and neural activity.

claim: The time constants estimated from spiking activity might not be linearly related to those estimated from fMRI.
source: (2) the time constants estimated from spiking activity might not be linearly related to those estimated from fMRI.
evidence: This is stated as a potential complication for interpretation.

claim: The exact relationship between timescales derived from spiking activity, LFPs and the BOLD signal remains an empirical question.
source: The exact relationship between timescales derived from spiking activity, LFPs and the BOLD signal remains an empirical question.
evidence: This is stated as an open question in the field.

claim: Hemodynamic timescales generally increase monotonically with those estimated from electrophysiology.
source: We hypothesize that hemodynamic timescales generally increase monotonically with those estimated from electrophysiology.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis.

claim: Timescales derived from electroencephalography (EEG) and fMRI have been shown to differ by 2 orders of magnitude.
source: In that respect, Watanabe et al., 2019 bring preliminary evidence—that is, timescales derived from electroencephalography (EEG) and fMRI have been shown to differ by 2 orders of magnitude.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Watanabe et al., 2019.

claim: When convolved with the hemodynamic response function, the INTs estimated from EEG were similar in magnitude to those estimated from fMRI.
source: This is reasonable considering the BOLD time course—when convolved with the hemodynamic response function, the INTs estimated from EEG were similar in magnitude to those estimated from fMRI.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from Watanabe et al., 2019.

claim: Temporal hierarchies are a general principle of organization, irrespective of the method used to estimate them.
source: Nevertheless, we show that temporal hierarchies are a general principle of organization, irrespective of the method used to estimate them.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Areas along the dorsal visual pathway follow the INT hierarchical ordering predicted by functional specialization and connectivity.
source: Remarkably, areas along the dorsal visual pathway follow the INT hierarchical ordering predicted by functional specialization and connectivity (Kravitz et al., 2011), with primary visual areas showing the fastest timescales and prefrontal areas showing the longest.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the dorsal visual pathway, supported by citation.

claim: The findings bring further evidence that the dorsal pathway is not a unitary system, but rather subdivided into multiple parallel pathways.
source: Our findings bring further evidence that the dorsal pathway is not a unitary system, but rather subdivided into multiple parallel pathways (Binkofski and Buxbaum, 2013; Kravitz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference from the findings, supported by citations.

claim: INT topographies are closely related to the overlapping FC gradient dimensions.
source: We show that INT topographies are closely related to the overlapping FC gradient dimensions.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the gradient analyses.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated that FC gradient dimensions in sensory cortex corresponded with known organizational principles such as eccentricity and polar angle.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that FC gradient dimensions in sensory cortex corresponded with known organizational principles such as eccentricity and polar angle (Haak et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Haak et al., 2018.

claim: FC gradients followed M1's somatotopic map.
source: Moreover, FC gradients followed M1's somatotopic map.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work.

claim: The findings put forward a significantly more unified framework that generalizes over the entire brain.
source: Our findings put forward a significantly more unified framework that generalizes over the entire brain.
evidence: This is a claim about the significance of the findings.

claim: INTs form a topographic organizational principle ranging from sensory to associative cortex.
source: INTs form a topographic organizational principle ranging from sensory to associative cortex.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claim: Intrinsic timescales appear to be special in their general extent as an organizational principle.
source: While other organizational principles can and likely always will be represented across topographic networks of the brain, intrinsic timescales appear to be special in their general extent.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the significance of INTs as an organizational principle.

claim: There are crucial methodological differences between the gradient and INT estimation approaches.
source: It is noteworthy that there are crucial methodological differences between the gradient and INT estimation approaches
evidence: This is stated as a methodological consideration.

claim: The gradient estimation pipeline consists of multiple steps to reduce the dimensionality of the data and consequently the amount of noise.
source: (1) the gradient estimation pipeline consists of multiple steps to reduce the dimensionality of the data, and consequently, the amount of noise (e.g., the FC matrix was made sparse; applying the cosine similarity kernel to build an affinity matrix; and applying a nonlinear dimensionality reduction technique to estimate the gradients)
evidence: This describes the gradient estimation methodology.

claim: The gradients were estimated bilaterally.
source: (2) the gradients were estimated bilaterally.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice.

claim: The INT measure consists of the temporal autocorrelation of individual voxels with no extra steps for noise reduction.
source: In comparison to gradients, where the spatial correlation between the voxels' time series is just the initial step in the pipeline, the INT measure consists of the temporal autocorrelation of individual voxels. No extra steps have been taken for noise reduction.
evidence: This describes the INT estimation methodology.

claim: There is a higher amount of variability in the INT maps which could potentially lead to the underestimation of the FC-INT relationship.
source: As a result, there is a higher amount of variability in the INT maps which could potentially lead to the underestimation of the FC-INT relationship.
evidence: This is stated as a potential limitation of the INT approach.

claim: The symmetry of the gradients could be a byproduct of estimating the gradients bilaterally.
source: With respect to the second point, the symmetry of the gradients could be a byproduct of estimating the gradients bilaterally.
evidence: This is stated as a potential methodological artifact.

claim: Other studies have derived gradients for each hemisphere individually and no major asymmetries have been reported.
source: Other studies e.g., Haak et al., 2018; Przezdzik et al., 2019 have derived gradients for each hemisphere individually and no major asymmetries have been reported.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The gradients were estimated bilaterally because RF transmit field (B1) inhomogeneities at ultrahigh fields lead to asymmetric signal intensities.
source: We estimated the gradients bilaterally because of an issue that is inherent with experimental ultrahigh fields. Specifically, RF transmit field (or B1) inhomogeneities lead to asymmetric signal intensities.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the methodological choice.

claim: Estimating gradients bilaterally partially addresses B1 inhomogeneity effects, but INTs are still susceptible to these effects.
source: We have reason to believe that this issue is partially being taken care of by estimating the gradients bilaterally, but the INTs are still susceptible to these effects.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological consideration.

claim: B1 inhomogeneity effects could result in the underestimation of the FC-INT relationship since there are visible asymmetries in the INT maps.
source: This could also result in the underestimation of the FC-INT relationship since there are visible asymmetries in the INT maps.
evidence: This is stated as a potential limitation.

claim: The anesthesia protocol used demonstrates no observable biases to whole-brain connectivity analysis.
source: It is important to note that it was previously shown that our anesthesia protocol demonstrates no observable biases to whole-brain connectivity analysis (Yacoub et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yacoub et al., 2020.

claim: The anesthesia protocol has a relatively low impact on reproducibility.
source: Moreover, it has been shown that this protocol has a relatively low impact on reproducibility (Autio et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Autio et al., 2021.

claim: The largest effect of vasodilative anesthetics (such as isoflurane) is an overall blunting of responses which is counteracted by ultrahigh field MRI.
source: To our knowledge, the largest effect of vasodilative anesthetics (such as isoflurane) is an overall blunting of responses which is counteracted by ultrahigh field MRI.
evidence: This is stated as knowledge about anesthesia effects.

claim: In anesthetized subjects, the confound of subjects engaging in various cognitive processes is potentially removed.
source: Finally, besides the possible effects on the hemodynamic response, anesthesia introduces a crucial difference between the current study and previous research—while in previous studies, it was not controlled for the subjects engaging in various cognitive processes, in anesthetized subjects, this confound is potentially removed.
evidence: This is stated as a potential advantage of using anesthesia.

claim: Future research should replicate current results to exclude a possible effect of anesthesia.
source: Overall, future research should replicate current results to exclude a possible effect of anesthesia.
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation for future work.

claim: Resting-state fMRI in NHPs is crucial for bridging the gap between human and animal models, and across various techniques of investigating the brain.
source: We show that resting-state fMRI in NHPs is crucial for bridging the gap between human and animal models, but also across the various techniques of investigating the brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the significance of the approach.

claim: Macaques have a disadvantage as a model organism for fMRI because of their small head size (~6% of the human brain) which makes the use of standard field strength magnets problematic for acquiring high-resolution data.
source: Nevertheless, macaques have a disadvantage as a model organism for fMRI because of their small head size (~6% of the human brain) which makes the use of standard field strength magnets problematic for acquiring high-resolution data.
evidence: This is stated as a challenge in macaque neuroimaging.

claim: Collecting high-resolution, high SNR whole-brain data in macaques has been extremely difficult.
source: As a result, collecting high-resolution, high SNR whole-brain data has been extremely difficult (Yacoub et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yacoub et al., 2020.

claim: One way of overcoming the problem of acquiring high-resolution data in macaques is to use ultrahigh field strengths in combination with high channel count receiver arrays.
source: We show here that one way of overcoming this problem is to use ultrahigh field strengths in combination with high channel count receiver arrays (Lagore et al., 2021; Uğurbil et al., 2019; Yacoub et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to technical developments.

claim: Ultrahigh magnetic fields not only enhance SNR but also increase the BOLD contrast, especially for the microvascular BOLD contributions.
source: Ultrahigh magnetic fields not only enhance SNR but also increase the BOLD contrast, especially for the microvascular BOLD contributions—which leads to mapping signals with higher precision to sites of neuronal activity (Ugurbil, 2016; Uğurbil, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ugurbil, 2016 and Uğurbil, 2018.

claim: The unique approach made it possible to obtain whole-brain high-resolution data to investigate FC and INTs across both cortical and subcortical structures.
source: In conclusion, our unique approach made it possible to obtain whole-brain high-resolution data to investigate FC and INTs across both cortical and subcortical structures.
evidence: This is a summary of the methodological contribution.

claim: INTs, like AC and FC, are one way of characterizing the organization of the brain.
source: INTs, like AC and FC, are one way of characterizing the organization of the brain.
evidence: This is stated as a conceptual framework.

claim: Combined maps of AC, FC, and INTs will require a nonhuman animal model such as the macaque, as AC cannot be directly measured in humans.
source: Critically, combined maps of all three will require a nonhuman animal model such as the macaque, as AC cannot be directly measured in humans (Grier et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Grier et al., 2020.

claim: AC, FC, and INTs are related, although the precise nature of the relationships is somewhat speculative.
source: It is clear that AC, FC, and INTs are related, although the precise nature of the relationships is somewhat speculative.
evidence: This is stated as current understanding in the field.

claim: Vertex FC strength is related to human INTs estimated from fMRI.
source: For instance, vertex FC strength is related to human INTs estimated from fMRI (Raut et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Raut et al., 2020.

claim: Cortico-striatal INTs and FC gradients broadly track AC.
source: Our own results show that cortico-striatal INTs and FC gradients broadly track AC.
evidence: This is a finding from the cortico-striatal analysis.

claim: AC establishes the pathways which the signals underpinning FC use.
source: AC establishes the pathways which the signals underpinning FC use.
evidence: This is stated as a conceptual relationship.

claim: Through cascaded processing, longer and longer TRWs can be built, measured as longer INTs.
source: Through cascaded processing, longer and longer TRWs can be built, measured as longer INTs.
evidence: This is stated as a mechanistic explanation.

claim: The space of potential INTs is constrained by both AC and FC.
source: Thus, we expect that the space of potential INTs is constrained by both AC and FC.
evidence: This is stated as an expectation based on the relationships observed.

claim: Future exploration of organizational principles, including using pharmacological interventions and electrical stimulation, will likely clarify the causal relationships at play.
source: Future exploration of these organizational principles, including using pharmacological interventions and electrical stimulation, will likely clarify the causal relationships at play.
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation for future research.

claim: Data were obtained from nine adult macaque monkeys (Macaca fascicularis: five female, and Macaca mulatta, three male and one female).
source: We obtained data from nine adult macaque monkeys (Macaca fascicularis: five female, and Macaca mulatta, three male and one female).
evidence: This describes the study sample.

claim: All data were acquired on a passively shielded 10.5 T, 88-cm diameter clear bore magnet.
source: All data were acquired on a passively shielded 10.5 T, 88-cm diameter clear bore magnet coupled to Siemens gradients ('SC72' body gradients operating at a slew rate of 200 mT/m/s, and 70 mT/m maximal strength), and electronics (Magnetom 10.5 T Plus) (Siemens, Erlangen, Germany).
evidence: This describes the imaging equipment used.

claim: Five to six runs of fMRI time series, each consisting of 700 continuous 2D multiband (MB)/Simultaneous Multi SLice (SMS) EPI functional volumes were acquired.
source: Five to six runs of fMRI time series, each consisting of 700 continuous 2D multiband (MB)/Simultaneous Multi SLice (SMS) EPI (Moeller et al., 2010; Setsompop et al., 2012; Uğurbil et al., 2013) functional volumes (TR=1110 ms; TE=17.6 ms; flip angle=60°, slices=58, matrix=108×154; FOV=81×115.5 mm2; acquisition voxel size=0.75×0.75×0.75 mm3) were acquired.
evidence: This describes the fMRI acquisition parameters.

claim: INTs were calculated by estimating the magnitude of the autocorrelation of the preprocessed functional data.
source: Based on previous studies (Murray et al., 2014; Watanabe et al., 2019), INTs were calculated by estimating the magnitude of the autocorrelation of the preprocessed functional data.
evidence: This describes the INT calculation method, supported by citations.

claim: The INT of each voxel was quantified as the sum of ACF values in the initial positive period.
source: At the single-subject level, the INT of each voxel was quantified as follows. For each run, the ACF of each voxel's fMRI signal was estimated. The ACF is the correlation of yt (time series) and yt+k (lagged time series), where k represents the time lag in steps of TR. Next, the sum of ACF values was calculated in the initial positive period. The upper limit of this period was set at the point where the ACF first becomes negative as the time lag increases. The result was used as an index of the INT of the brain region.
evidence: This describes the INT quantification method.

claim: FC gradients were computed using BrainSpace, a toolbox for the identification, visualization, and analysis of macroscale gradients in neuroimaging data sets.
source: We computed FC gradients using BrainSpace, a toolbox for the identification, visualization, and analysis of macroscale gradients in neuroimaging data sets (Vos de Wael et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the gradient computation method, supported by a citation.
